name: Design a Key Management Service
intent: Let hundreds of services encrypt their data without ever holding a master key: wrap data keys in a key hierarchy rooted in hardware, rotate keys without re-encrypting everything, restrict and audit every use, replicate across regions, and survive being the dependency of everything.
codeTitle: envelope encryption with versions, policy and audit
finalIntro: One service saving an encrypted card number, reading it back months later, and the key being rotated in between.
prompt: Design a key management service for a company with hundreds of services in several regions. Teams need to encrypt data at rest, such as card numbers, documents and database backups, without handling the master keys. Keys must be rotated regularly, every use must be restricted by policy and written to an audit log, and the root of trust must be in hardware. When a key is deleted, the data under it becomes unreadable for good, so deletion must be safe. Almost every request in the company will depend on this service.
functional: Create keys, with a name, a policy and a rotation schedule
Generate a data key and return it both in plain form and wrapped by a named key
Decrypt a wrapped data key for an authorised caller
Rotate a key to a new version while old data stays readable
Rewrap a wrapped data key under the newest version without exposing it
Disable a key, and delete it only after a waiting period that can be cancelled
Record every use in an audit log that cannot be edited
Make keys usable in every region
nonFunctional: A data key is wrapped or unwrapped in under 10 ms inside a region, at tens of thousands of calls per second
The service is more available than any service that uses it, with a target of 99.99% or better
Master key material never exists outside hardware in plain form
A caller can do only what its policy allows, and every call, allowed or denied, is logged
Rotation never requires re-encrypting bulk data
A key cannot be destroyed by a single mistake or a single person
Keys keep working when one region is lost, and policy changes reach every region within seconds

firstAttempt.text: One secret key kept in each service's configuration. A service encrypts every record with it directly and stores the ciphertext in the database. To change the key, a team edits the configuration and redeploys.
limits: The key is copied into every deployment, backup and laptop that touches the configuration, so anyone who reads it can decrypt everything
Changing the key means re-encrypting every record, so in practice it never changes
There is no record of who used the key, and no way to give one service less power than another
Deleting the configuration by accident destroys the key and with it all the data
Each team invents its own scheme, and some of them get the cryptography wrong

steps.title: Encrypt with data keys, and wrap those with a key service
steps.problem: A shared secret copied into every service is both a huge target and impossible to change, and sending all the data to a central service to be encrypted would make that service the bottleneck for every byte.
steps.fix: Use envelope encryption. A service asks the KMS for a fresh data key. The KMS returns it twice: once in plain form, and once wrapped (encrypted) by a named key that never leaves the KMS. The service encrypts its data locally with the plain key, stores the ciphertext together with the wrapped key, and forgets the plain key. To read, it sends the wrapped key back and receives the plain key. Only small keys of about 32 bytes cross the network, never the data, and every object can have its own data key.
steps.tradeoff: The KMS handles tiny requests and the bulk work stays in the services, so it scales to enormous data volumes. Every read and write of protected data now needs a data key, which is a dependency on the KMS, and the stored wrapped key adds about a hundred bytes to each object.

steps.title: Build a hierarchy, with a root key in hardware
steps.problem: If the keys in the KMS are stored in a database as they are, then whoever can read the database, a backup or a dump, owns every key in the company.
steps.fix: Keys form a hierarchy. A root key lives inside a hardware security module (HSM), a tamper-resistant device that does cryptography but will not export the key. The root key wraps the key-encryption keys (KEKs), which are the named keys that teams use. A KEK wraps data keys. The key store holds only wrapped keys. To unwrap a KEK the KMS asks the HSM, which does it inside the hardware. The root key is created in a ceremony and backed up in pieces, so a quorum of several trusted people is needed to restore it.
steps.tradeoff: Stealing the database or its backups gets an attacker only ciphertext, and the one secret that matters sits in hardware. The HSM is a scarce, slower, costlier resource with a limited number of operations per second, so the KMS unwraps each KEK rarely and keeps it in memory, and the root key's backups and ceremony are real operational work.

steps.title: Version the keys so rotation does not touch the data
steps.problem: Keys should be replaced regularly and after any suspected leak, but re-encrypting petabytes of data to do it is too slow and risky to ever happen.
steps.fix: A key has numbered versions. Rotating creates a new version, which is used for all new wrapping, and older versions stay available only for decrypting. Each wrapped data key records the version that sealed it, so the KMS picks the right one. Because the data is encrypted with data keys and only those small keys are wrapped by the KEK, a background job can rewrap old data keys under the newest version, leaving the bulk data untouched. When no wrapped key refers to an old version, it can be retired.
steps.tradeoff: Rotation is cheap and routine, and a compromised version stops protecting new data at once. Old versions must be kept until everything has been rewrapped, rewrapping many billions of keys takes days and consumes KMS capacity, and rotating a data key itself, rather than its wrapper, does still mean re-encrypting that object.

steps.title: Check a policy for every call, and log every call
steps.problem: Without limits, any service that can reach the KMS could decrypt any other team's data, and after a breach nobody could say what was read.
steps.fix: Every key has a policy that names who may do what: encrypt, decrypt, rewrap, or administer, often only from certain services, networks or accounts. Callers prove who they are with short-lived workload identities, and the policy check runs before any key is touched, with deny as the default. Administration is split from use, so the people who manage a key cannot decrypt with it. Each call, allowed or denied, is appended to an audit log with the caller, key, version, time and outcome, and entries are chained by hashes so that a change to an old entry can be detected.
steps.tradeoff: A leaked credential exposes only what its policy allows, and investigators can reconstruct exactly which keys were used. Policies need careful design and review, the check adds a little latency to every call, and an audit log that records every use is itself a huge, sensitive stream that must be stored for years.

steps.title: Replicate keys to every region, and cache so an outage does not stop the world
steps.problem: Services in every region need keys with low latency, a lost region must not make its data unreadable, and because everything depends on the KMS, a KMS outage would stop everything at once.
steps.fix: Key metadata and wrapped key material are copied to each region, where a local HSM holds its own root key and a replicated key is wrapped again for that region. Policy changes and new versions are replicated within seconds and callers use their local KMS. Services keep recently unwrapped data keys in a short-lived cache in memory, and the KMS servers keep unwrapped KEKs in memory, so most calls do not travel to the KMS or the HSM at all. During an outage a service can keep using cached keys for reads, and fail over to another region if the problem is only local.
steps.tradeoff: Reads are fast, and a lost region or a short outage hurts much less. A cache means a disabled key keeps working for as long as the cache lives, replication lag means a brand new version may not be there yet, and a fault that hits all regions together, such as a bad policy rollout, is not helped by replicas.

steps.title: Delete keys only after a waiting period
steps.problem: Destroying a key makes all data under it unreadable for ever, so a mistake, a script gone wrong or an attacker with admin rights could wipe out a whole service's data in a second.
steps.fix: Deleting is a request, not an action. The key goes into a pending-deletion state for a waiting period, commonly 7 to 30 days, during which it cannot be used and any attempt to use it raises an alert. Anyone with the right role can cancel the deletion, and the key then returns to service. Only when the period ends does a job destroy the key material, and for the most valuable keys the request needs approval from two administrators. Disabling a key first is the safe way to find out what still depends on it.
steps.tradeoff: A mistake can be undone for days, and an attacker or a bad script cannot cause instant, permanent loss. Real deletion, such as a customer's right to be forgotten or the removal of a tenant, is delayed by the waiting period, and the key's storage cost continues until then.

failures.scenario: The KMS in one region is unavailable for twenty minutes
failures.impact: Every service that must unwrap a data key to read or save data starts to fail, and a failure in a security service looks like a failure of the whole company.
failures.answer: Services keep recently used data keys in a short-lived cache, so most reads continue. Calls that miss the cache fail over to the nearest healthy region, which has a replica of the key, at the price of extra latency. Services use timeouts and retries with backoff, so a recovering KMS is not flooded by every client at the same moment, and requests that cannot be served are rejected quickly rather than queued.

failures.scenario: Someone schedules a production key for deletion, or a script deletes keys by mistake
failures.impact: If the key were destroyed at once, the data under it would be gone for ever, and backups would not help because they are encrypted with the same key.
failures.answer: The key is only pending deletion for the waiting period. Calls to use it fail with a clear error and raise an alert on the first attempt, which is usually how the mistake is noticed. An administrator cancels the deletion and the key returns with all its versions. Important keys also need a second approval to schedule deletion.

failures.impact: The attacker can call the KMS as that service and decrypt whatever it is allowed to decrypt.
failures.answer: The policy limits the damage to the keys that service used. Workload identities expire in minutes, so the stolen credential stops working soon. Anomaly alerts fire on unusual volume or an unusual source network, and the audit log shows exactly which keys and wrapped data keys were unwrapped, so the affected objects are known. The key can be rotated, and the service's access revoked, in seconds.

failures.scenario: A new key version is used in one region before it has been replicated to another
failures.impact: Data wrapped under version 6 in region A cannot be decrypted in region B, which has only version 5, so reads there fail.
failures.answer: New versions are replicated first and made the active version only after every region confirms it holds the version. The wrapped key records its version, so a region that lacks it can fetch it on demand from the home region, and a caller that gets 'unknown version' retries rather than treating the data as lost.

failures.scenario: The HSM that holds the root key fails, or the people who hold its backup shares are unavailable
failures.impact: Without the root key no key can be unwrapped, so all data in the region is unreadable.
failures.answer: Root keys live in a cluster of HSMs that share the key, so one device failing changes nothing. A backup of the root key is split between several people, and any quorum of them can restore it, so no single person is a point of failure or a point of theft. The restore procedure is rehearsed, and KEKs held in the memory of running KMS servers keep traffic going meanwhile.

alternatives.title: Where the encryption of data happens

options.name: The KMS encrypts the data itself
options.pro: Services never see any key, and the logic is trivial
options.con: All data crosses the network, and the KMS becomes the bottleneck for every byte

options.name: Envelope encryption with data keys
options.pro: Only 32-byte keys travel, services encrypt locally, and rotation rewraps small keys
options.con: Services handle plain data keys in memory, and each object stores a wrapped key

options.name: Keys fetched once and used for a long time
options.con: Back to a long-lived secret in every service, and slow to rotate or revoke

alternatives.pick: Envelope encryption, with data keys cached for a short time.

alternatives.title: The root of trust

options.name: Software keys in a protected file
options.con: Anyone who can read the file or the machine's memory can copy the key

options.name: A cluster of HSMs
options.pro: The key cannot be exported, and operations are logged by the hardware
options.con: Costly, limited throughput, and needs ceremonies and backups

options.name: A cloud provider's managed HSM
options.pro: No hardware to run, and standard certifications
options.con: Trust in the provider, and some lock-in

alternatives.pick: HSMs at the root, with software only for the layers below that hold wrapped keys.

alternatives.title: How to rotate

options.name: Re-encrypt all data under a new key
options.pro: Nothing refers to the old key afterwards
options.con: Petabytes of work for each rotation, so it is skipped

options.name: New version, and lazily rewrap data keys
options.pro: Cheap, and the new version protects new data at once
options.con: Old versions have to stay until the rewrap has finished

options.name: Never rotate
options.con: A leak is permanent, and compliance rules usually forbid it

alternatives.pick: Versioned keys with automatic yearly rotation and a background rewrap, and a full re-encryption only after a real compromise.

alternatives.title: Keys across regions

options.name: One home region for each key
options.pro: Simple, and no copies to protect
options.con: Every other region depends on a distant region, and a regional failure is a global one for that key

options.name: Replicate each key to every region that needs it
options.pro: Local calls, and a lost region is survivable
options.con: More copies to protect and keep consistent

options.name: Independent keys in each region
options.con: Data cannot move between regions without being re-encrypted

alternatives.pick: Replicate to the regions that need a key, and make the home region the only place where administration happens.

quiz.question: A service must encrypt 1 GB database backups every night and cannot hold the master key. A developer proposes sending each backup to the KMS to encrypt it there. What is the better design?
options: Ask the KMS once for the master key and keep it in the memory of the service, to encrypt all the backups locally and avoid any further calls
Send the backup to the KMS in 4 KB chunks, so that each chunk is encrypted under a key that never leaves it
Encrypt backups with a single shared key stored in the secrets manager, and rotate it every year by redeploying
Ask the KMS for a data key in plain and wrapped form, encrypt locally, store the wrapped key with the file, and discard the plain key
quiz.explanation: Envelope encryption moves only a 32-byte key across the network, and the bulk work stays in the service. Fetching the master key breaks the rule that it never leaves the KMS, chunking would push every byte through the KMS and make it the bottleneck, and a shared key brings back the problems of a copied secret.

quiz.question: At the yearly routine rotation of a key-encryption key, there are 4 billion wrapped data keys under version 6, protecting 3 petabytes of data. A background job can rewrap 20,000 keys per second. When can version 6 be retired, and what must be re-encrypted?
options: After about 2.3 days of rewrapping the wrapped keys under the new version, with the data left untouched
Immediately, because new data keys are already wrapped under version 7, and the old data is covered by the same key
After about 2.3 days, once the 3 petabytes of data have also been re-encrypted under new data keys from version 7
Never, because wrapped keys keep their original version, so old versions have to stay available in case they are read
quiz.explanation: 4 billion / 20,000 per second is 200,000 seconds, about 2.3 days, and only the small wrapped keys need rewrapping, because the data is encrypted by data keys. Retiring version 6 at once would make old wrapped keys undecryptable. Re-encrypting the bulk data is needed only after a real compromise.

quiz.question: Region A creates version 6 of a key and starts wrapping new data keys with it at once. Replication to region B takes a few seconds. For that time, reads in region B of data wrapped in region A fail with 'unknown version'. What is the correct change?
options: Raise the cache time of unwrapped data keys in region B, so that its services keep reading during the replication lag
Let region B try to decrypt with version 5 whenever version 6 is missing, since both versions come from the same key
Replicate a new version first, activate it when every region confirms, and let regions fetch unknown ones on demand
Make region A the only home for the key, so that every region always sends its unwrap requests there instead
quiz.explanation: A version must exist everywhere before anything is wrapped with it. Longer caching hides only keys already read, and version 5 cannot unwrap a key wrapped by version 6. A single home region removes the lag but makes each other region depend on a distant one, so a regional failure becomes a global one for that key.
